To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the prevalence of hepatitis C infection in patients undergoing liver transplantation for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) has declined from 30% in the early 1990s to 5% in 2006.

we identified 4, 3- and 2-year survival rates of 75.5% (95% confidence interval, 72.0-79.1), 56.0% (95% CI, 50.9-61.2) and 41.7% (95%CI, 35.7-47.8), respectively, in patients undergoing diaphragmatic resections with a 3.5-year median follow-up.
the incidence of HCC with diaphragmatic invasion has increased over recent years, and that diaphragmatic invasion does not preclude surgical cure.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a new approach to the study of the structure of the diaphragm and its function in breathing.
the development of an integrated system for the management of patients with hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) and cirrhosis.
the development of new and efficient numerical methods for solving partial differential equations.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the use of a single agent, or combination of drugs, in the treatment of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is still not established, and further studies are needed to clarify the efficacy of these agents.

, although there are no randomized controlled studies to date to support the efficacy and safety of the use of antiviral drugs in the management of chronic hepatitis C patients with advanced fibrosis, the use of antihistone HCV drugs may have a role in the treatment of these patients, especially those with advanced fibrosis and compensated liver disease.
the evidence does not suggest a causal relationship between hepatitis B virus (HBV) or hepatitis C virus (HCV) and the development of hepatocellular carcinoma.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we are able to identify and characterize the most common genetic alterations in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC).
the use of a 3D printed model is a valuable and effective method to assist in the surgical management of complex hepatic lesions.
the use of a 2D/3D approach in the planning process of a patient with hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) and portal vein thrombosis is feasible and safe.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of a novel technique for the management of hepatic tumors involving the diaphragm, the en bloc resection of the diaphragm along with a hepatic resection, is feasible and safe.
we can now use a combination of genetic testing and clinical data to predict the risk of recurrence of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC).
the risk of developing hepatocellular carcinoma is increased in patients with NAFLD and NASH compared with the general population.
